title: Hyper optimizing Kimi K3 in vLLM: moving fast and responsibly
gist: Coding agents helped write a fused decode path for one model on one chip, merged into vLLM. The post's real subject is process: agent-written optimisations now arrive faster than maintainers can read them, so it proposes isolating them in per-model directories and having reviewers judge evidence (full-model evaluations plus kernel tests) instead of every line.
changes: Public, merged proof that agent-written kernel work is in the main open engine, and an admission that human review is now the queue. Also the opposite bet to Together's on megakernels, in the same month.
caveats: Agent-assisted, not autonomous; the loop is not described. Decode numbers exclude prefill, and the speculation figure uses a synthetic acceptance length. The AgentX gain of 1.8x compares 16 GPUs with an earlier run on 8. Standalone kernel tests missed a compiler reordering bug and numerical issues that only long evaluations caught. A reviewer's remark about unread kernel code comes from the pull request, read second-hand.

numbers.metric: Per-layer decode, Kimi K3 on GB300
numbers.value: about 130 microseconds and 23 kernels, down to 69 and 13

numbers.baseline: stock vLLM with the same speculation settings
numbers.setup: 16 GB300s, seven draft tokens, acceptance length fixed at 6, prefill excluded

bears_on.note: Agent-written kernel code, merged upstream, with model-level evaluations attached.
Review capacity is the stated limit, and the existing test gates missed real bugs.
The work landed in the commons the day it was announced.
